sections.executive_summary:
Texas licenses assisted living facilities (ALFs) under the Assisted Living Facility Licensing Act (Health & Safety Code Chapter 247) and 26 TAC Chapter 553, administered by HHSC Long-term Care Regulation [S13]. There are two license types. **Type A** residents can evacuate without staff help and don't need routine attendance at night. **Type B** residents may need help evacuating, help transferring, or attendance at night, but may not be permanently bedfast [S1]. A facility is **small** at 16 or fewer licensed residents and **large** at 17 or more [S2].

Money comes mainly from private pay. NCAL reports 2,003 Texas assisted living communities with 82,881 beds/units, and only 8% of residents rely on Medicaid for their long-term care [S27]. CareScout's 2025 Texas median for assisted living is $67,992 a year ($5,666/month) for a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community [S26]. Medicaid assisted living is paid through **STAR+PLUS** managed care. MCOs pay the facility a daily rate (HHSC's published 9/1/2025 rates are $44.82–$74.04/day by setting and level), and the resident pays room and board of SSI minus an $85 allowance, which is $909/month in 2026 [S20][S22][S24].

Licensing is cheap and fairly quick. The license fee is $300 plus $15 per bed for three years [S3]. After the building passes HHSC's Life Safety Code inspection you may admit 1–3 residents before the health inspection, and HHSC issues the license within 30 days of finding all requirements met [S7][S6]. The costly parts are the building (new small facilities must be sprinklered) [S10][S11] and 24-hour staffing — Type B and large facilities need awake night staff [S5].

**Bottom line from the model.** At 88% occupancy, the 16-bed private-pay Type B facility nets about $24,700/month, the best result in the model. The 40-unit large facility with 20% STAR+PLUS nets about $17,900/month once rent is sized for apartment units (each at least a studio with its own bath and kitchen), only about $3,800 at 80% occupancy, and needs about 78% occupancy to break even. A 6-bed private-pay Type B home with a paid manager and the on-call nurse needed to administer medications nets only about $1,900/month and loses about $500 at 80% — it works best when the owner is the manager. Mixing STAR+PLUS beds into a 6-bed home makes it lose money; in a 16-bed home it still nets about $8,100/month.

### What this report does not claim
- MCO contract rates paid to specific ALFs (the published HHSC rates are used).
- Small-home or shared-room private-pay rates (the $5,666 median is for a private one-bedroom in an AL community).
- Texas-only occupancy, competitor names, market shares or provider counts by city.
- A liability insurance minimum or generator mandate (none found in the rules reviewed).
- Rent for 16- and 40-bed buildings (operator estimates built from HUD Small Area FMRs: per-bed house rent for 16 beds; one studio per unit for 40 units, excluding common areas).
sections.service_model:
### Who is served
Texas ALFs serve adults who need help with daily living but not continuous nursing. NCAL's Texas profile shows 71% of residents are women, 51% are 85 or older, 69% need help bathing, 62% need help dressing and 43% have Alzheimer's disease or dementia [S27]. "Personal care services" in the rule means help with feeding, dressing, moving, bathing or other personal needs, plus general supervision [S2].

### License types
| Type | Who can live there | Night staff |
|---|---|---|
| Type A, small (≤16) | Can evacuate without staff help; no routine night attendance; can follow directions in an emergency [S1] | Immediately available (may be asleep) [S5] |
| Type A, large (17+) | Same as above | Immediately available and awake [S5] |
| Type B (any size) | May need evacuation help, night attendance or transfer help; not permanently bedfast [S1] | Immediately available and awake [S5] |

Most new residential homes license as **small Type B**, because residents' needs rise over time and a Type A home must discharge residents who can no longer self-evacuate. Only a Type B facility (or a Type B unit) can earn **Alzheimer's certification** (26 TAC §553.27), which carries an extra $300 per 3-year license [S50][S3]. HHSC still lists a Type C (four-bed adult foster care) license, but for renewals only [S4].

### Zoning: the 6-resident line
Under the Community Homes for Disabled Persons Location Act, an ALF licensed under HSC Chapter 247 qualifies as a "community home" if its exterior stays compatible with nearby houses [S17]. A community home may house no more than six persons with disabilities plus two supervisors [S18], and it may not be within one-half mile of another community home [S19]. Above six residents, plan on local zoning approval.

### Medication services
Under PL 2023-22, medications may be **administered** only by a licensed nurse, an employee with an HHSC medication aide permit acting under a nurse on duty or on call, or an attendant to whom an RN delegated the task. Trained staff may also **supervise or assist** residents with self-administration (reminding, pouring prescribed doses, observing, documenting missed doses) [S14]. A medication aide permit takes 100 classroom hours, 20 lab hours and 10 clinical hours plus an exam, and is renewed every year [S15].

### Pending rule changes
On September 4, 2026, HHSC proposed a broad rewrite of Chapter 553 (Proposed Rule 25R031). It would require dedicated staff on each shift, bar sharing on-duty attendants with another facility, bar using family members or companion care providers to cover staffing shortages, extend the manager training exemption break from 30 to 90 days, add infection-control training, require accredited food handler courses, and renumber many sections. HHSC reports no fee changes [S16]. This report cites the current rules; check the adopted version before you apply.
sections.licensing_pathway:
### Step by step (26 TAC §553.23; HHSC "How to Become an ALF Provider")
1. **Pick the license type and size.** Type A or B, small (≤16) or large (17+) [S1][S2]. This choice sets night staffing, construction rules and whether STAR+PLUS non-apartment contracting is possible (16 or fewer beds, freestanding) [S5][S21].
2. **Check the site.** Zoning (6 or fewer residents is a protected community home with half-mile spacing) [S17][S18][S19]. In counties over 3.3 million residents (Harris County), new applications must not be in a 100-year floodplain [S9]. The building must meet Subchapter D for its category; **new small Type A and Type B facilities must have an NFPA 13, 13R or 13D sprinkler system** with electrical supervision and a manual fire alarm with smoke detection [S10][S11][S52]. New construction can get early HHSC plan review [S4].
3. **Form the entity and check owners.** Texas LLC Certificate of Formation (Form 205) costs $300 [S44]; get an EIN [S46]. HHSC must deny an applicant or controlling person who had a facility license revoked in the previous five years or is excluded from Medicare/Medicaid [S9].
4. **Complete HHSC's pre-licensure computer-based training** (about 1–2 hours) and keep the signed certificate. HHSC will not accept an application packet without it [S12][S7].
5. **Apply in TULIP.** Use Form 3720 (3721 adds Alzheimer's certification). Include documentation from the local fire authority that the facility meets local fire ordinances, ownership documents and the full fee [S4][S8]. The fee is **$300 + $15 per bed, capped at $2,250, for a 3-year license**, paid with the application: $390 for 6 beds, $540 for 16, $900 for 40 [S3]. Fees are nonrefundable except as the rule allows [S3].
6. **HHSC document review: within 30 days.** HHSC tells you if anything is missing. An application still incomplete 120 days after receipt is denied [S6].
7. **Life Safety Code inspection.** Tell HHSC through the portal that the building is ready, either with the application or within 120 days of HHSC receiving it. If the building still fails 120 days after the first LSC inspection, the application is denied [S7]. You may pay for an Expedited LSC inspection: the rule says it must occur no later than the 15th day after HHSC receives the request (§553.47(g)) [S3], while HHSC's web page says 15 business days [S4]. Check the current fee in §553.47(g) before requesting.
8. **Admit 1 to 3 residents.** After passing LSC you may admit at least one and no more than three residents [S7][S4].
9. **Health inspection.** Tell HHSC you are ready. HHSC inspects against Subchapter E (operations and resident care). Failing 120 days after the first health inspection means denial [S7].
10. **License issued** within 30 days after HHSC determines all requirements are met [S6]. HHSC's web page says 45 days [S4]; plan on the longer figure.

### Ongoing
- Renew every 3 years at the same fee. Filing later than 45 days before expiration adds a late fee of half the basic fee [S3].
- Each added bed costs $15 [S3].
- The manager must finish a 24-hour course by the first anniversary and 12 hours of CE each year [S5].
- Self-report incidents through TULIP or call Complaint and Incident Intake at 800-458-9858 [S47].
sections.reimbursement:
### Private pay (the main payer)
NCAL reports that only 8% of Texas assisted living residents rely on Medicaid [S27]. Most revenue is private pay, from personal funds, family, long-term care insurance or veterans' benefits. CareScout's 2025 Texas median is **$5,666/month ($67,992/yr)** for a private one-bedroom unit in an assisted living community, ranked 34th of 50 states [S26]. Small residential homes with shared rooms often price below this, so set your rate from local comparables.

### STAR+PLUS (Texas Medicaid managed care)
STAR+PLUS HCBS serves adults 21 and older who meet nursing facility level of care and Medicaid financial rules and choose community services [S23]. Assisted living is one of its services. Here is how the money flows:
1. **The member must live in an ALF that holds a contract with their STAR+PLUS MCO** [S21]. Each MCO credentials and contracts separately. Federal rules require states to screen and enroll every managed care network provider, so plan on Texas Medicaid (TMHP) enrollment as well [S51].
2. **The MCO pays a daily rate.** HHSC's 9/1/2025 rate sheet lists T2031 assisted living rates of **$67.18–$74.04/day for single-occupancy apartments**, $55.78–$66.97 for double-occupancy apartments, and **$44.82–$63.16/day for non-apartment settings**, across six PDPM-based levels (PDPM replaced the RUG-III payment model on 9/1/2025). Providers keep billing a member's old RUG-III code until that member's individual service plan (ISP) renews, then switch to T2031; claims with the wrong code are denied [S57]. Each rate includes a $37.52 attendant component built on a $13.00/hour attendant wage [S20][S58].
3. **The resident pays room and board** equal to the SSI federal benefit rate minus an $85 personal needs allowance [S22]: **$994 − $85 = $909/month in 2026** [S24]. It cannot be waived (the facility may accept less), and SSI recipients owe no copayment [S21].
4. **Setting rules matter.** An "apartment" needs a private bath and cooking facilities and at least 220 sq ft for single occupancy (160 sq ft in remodeled existing structures). A "non-apartment" unit must be in a freestanding building licensed for 16 or fewer beds [S21]. A typical 6–16 bed residential home bills the non-apartment rates.

**What a STAR+PLUS bed earns.** At the simple average of the six non-apartment levels ($53.44/day × 30.42) plus $909 room and board, a bed brings about **$2,535/month**. At the apartment single average ($70.47/day), it brings about **$3,053/month**. Both are well below the $5,666 private-pay median. STAR+PLUS providers must also accept MCO referrals when space is available, unless the member's condition is inappropriate under the license [S21].

**Interest list.** HHSC keeps a STAR+PLUS HCBS interest list for people not already enrolled in STAR+PLUS. People already enrolled in STAR+PLUS ask their MCO and do not wait on the list [S23][S25].

### Other payers
STAR+PLUS also pays respite in assisted living ($43.97–$61.05/day non-apartment) [S20]. Adult Foster Care ($19.19–$67.20/day) is a competing low-cost STAR+PLUS residential option [S20].

- **Population.** Texas had an estimated 31.7 million residents on July 1, 2025, and 14.9% were 65 or older [S29].
- **Resident profile.** 51% of Texas assisted living residents are 85 or older, 43% have Alzheimer's or dementia, 69% need help bathing and 63% need help walking [S27]. These are the needs that make Type B licensing and memory care in demand.
- **Supply.** 2,003 communities and 82,881 beds/units statewide [S27].
- **Occupancy.** Assisted living occupancy in NIC's 31 primary markets reached 88.4% in 2Q 2026 [S28]. No free Texas-only figure was found.
- **Medicaid pipeline.** STAR+PLUS members who meet nursing facility level of care can use assisted living through their MCO without waiting on the interest list; others go on HHSC's interest list [S23][S25]. The 2022–23 legislative release allocated 107 STAR+PLUS HCBS interest-list slots [S25].

**Referral sources** (operator practice): hospital and rehab discharge planners, home health and hospice agencies, geriatric care managers, placement agencies (fee per move-in), STAR+PLUS MCO service coordinators (for contracted facilities), Area Agencies on Aging, churches and senior centers. No sourced referral volumes are claimed.
sections.operations:
### Staffing rules (26 TAC §553.253)
- **An attendant must be in the facility whenever residents are present** [S5].
- **No numeric ratio.** Facilities must set staffing ratios based on residents' service plans, disclose the normal 24-hour staffing pattern before admission, and post it monthly. Staff must be sufficient to keep order, safety and cleanliness, help with medications, prepare meals, help with laundry, supervise residents and ensure safe evacuation [S5].
- **Night shift:** small Type A — immediately available. Large Type A and all Type B — **immediately available and awake** [S5][S14].
- **Manager:** on duty 40 hours a week and may manage only one facility. Managers of small Type A facilities may oversee up to four facilities with no more than 16 residents in total. A backup must be designated in writing [S5].
- **Manager qualifications:** small facility — high school diploma or equivalent. Large facility — an associate's degree in nursing, health care management or a related field, a bachelor's degree, or a high school credential plus one year of management experience [S5].

### Training
| Who | Requirement |
|---|---|
| All staff | 4 hours of orientation before any job duties [S5] |
| Attendants | 16 hours of supervised on-the-job training within the first 16 hours after orientation; first aid including Heimlich, falls and sudden changes in condition [S5] |
| Direct care staff | 6 documented hours a year, including 1 hour of fall prevention and 1 hour of behavior management [S5] |
| Manager | 24-hour ALF management course by first anniversary (8 hours on standards within 3 months); 12 hours CE a year [S5] |
| Medication aides | HHSC permit: 100 classroom + 20 lab + 10 clinical hours and exam; annual renewal; 7 hours of CE after the first renewal [S15] |

### Required systems and checks
- Criminal history and registry checks for employees under HSC Chapter 250 [S48].
- Sprinkler and fire alarm systems with ongoing testing and monitoring [S10][S11].
- Incident self-reports through TULIP [S47].
- STAR+PLUS providers must give each member a health assessment and emergency training within 3 days of admission, offer at least four social activities a week, and report significant changes to the MCO by the next business day [S21].

### Staffing used in the model
- **6-bed Type B:** one awake attendant on every shift (730 hrs/month), a 40-hr/week manager who works as a second person on days, and an LVN or RN on call (4 hrs/week) so medications can be administered by permitted medication aides or under RN delegation [S14].
- **16-bed Type B:** one attendant 24/7 plus a medication aide/shift lead on days and evenings (2 staff on days and evenings, 1 awake overnight), a 40-hr/week cook/housekeeper, an LVN on call (8 hrs/week) and the manager.
- **40-unit large Type B:** 4 staff on days, 3 on evenings, 2 awake overnight, a 40-hr/week LVN, cook, housekeeping, activities and a manager with large-facility qualifications.
sections.market_conditions:
- **Pricing.** Texas's private-pay assisted living median of $5,666/month ranks 34th of 50 states and sits below Oklahoma ($6,150) and above Florida ($5,610) in the same survey [S26]. Medicaid rates are far lower: a STAR+PLUS bed brings about $2,535 (non-apartment) to $3,053 (apartment) a month including room and board [S20][S22].
- **Medicaid share.** About 8% of residents rely on Medicaid [S27], so most facilities are private-pay businesses with a few STAR+PLUS beds at most.
- **Wages.** Texas follows the $7.25 federal minimum wage [S36][S37], but competitive caregiver pay is higher. BLS OEWS 2025 Texas wages: personal care aides median $11.65 and 75th percentile $13.23; nursing assistants median $18.03; LVNs $29.92; institutional cooks $17.00; housekeepers $14.26 [S30][S31][S32][S34][S35]. HHSC built its 9/1/2025 STAR+PLUS attendant rates on a $13.00 hourly wage [S20]. Metro wages run higher: the personal care aide median is $12.93 in Dallas-Fort Worth and $13.64 in Austin [S30].
- **Rent.** HUD FY2027 Small Area FMR for a 4-bedroom home: Dallas ZIP 75287 $3,190, Houston ZIP 77084 $2,840, San Antonio ZIP 78230 $2,330 [S41][S43][S42].
- **Regulatory trend.** Proposed Rule 25R031 (Sept. 2026) tightens shift staffing (dedicated on-duty staff, no shared attendants, no family members covering shortages) and adds food handler and infection-control training [S16]. Budget for that if it is adopted.
- **Taxes.** The Texas franchise tax no-tax-due threshold is $2,650,000 for 2026–2027 reports [S45]. Every modeled configuration is below it. New employers pay 2.70% state unemployment tax on the first $9,000 per worker [S39]. Workers' comp is elective in Texas [S38].
sections.financial_narrative:
### How the P&L is built
Revenue per resident × occupied residents, minus staffing (with payroll burden) and operating costs. Default occupancy is 88%, the NIC 2Q 2026 primary-market figure [S28]. The conservative case is 80% and the optimistic case 95%. Ramp-up: the 6-bed homes start at 1 resident and add 1 a month; the 16-bed starts at 2 and adds 2; the 40-unit starts at 4 and adds 3. These are operator planning assumptions — verify against your referral pipeline.

**Revenue.** Private pay uses the CareScout 2025 Texas median of $5,666/month [S26]. It measures a private one-bedroom unit in an AL community, so the 6- and 16-bed results may be optimistic. STAR+PLUS beds earn room and board of $909 [S22][S24] plus the published 9/1/2025 T2031 daily rate: the non-apartment average of $53.44/day for homes of 16 or fewer, or the apartment single average of $70.47/day for the 40-unit building [S20]. Replace these with your MCO contract rates.

**Staffing.** Every configuration has awake night staff (Type B) and an attendant on site at all times [S5]. Caregivers are paid $13.23/hr (Texas 75th-percentile personal care aide) [S30], above both the $7.25 minimum [S37] and the $13.00 wage HHSC used to build STAR+PLUS rates [S20][S58]. Medication aides are paid the nursing assistant median of $18.03 [S31], LVNs $29.92 [S32] (8 hrs/week on call in the 16-bed homes, 4 hrs/week in the 6-bed homes, 40 hrs/week in the 40-unit building — hours are operator estimates; a nurse is needed because only nurses, permitted medication aides under a nurse, or RN-delegated attendants may administer medications [S14]), and managers the Texas 10th percentile ($65,520) for small homes and 25th percentile ($86,080) for the large facility [S33]. Burden is 8.7% payroll taxes [S39][S40], plus 3% workers' comp and 5% benefits (both operator estimates).

**Operating costs.**
- Rent is fixed from day one. The 6- and 16-bed homes use $611.50 per licensed bed, from the Dallas HUD 4-bedroom SAFMR × 1.15 for a 5-bedroom home [S41]: 6 beds $3,669; 16 beds $9,784. The 40-unit building uses 40 × the Dallas FY2027 studio SAFMR of $1,640 = $65,600, because STAR+PLUS apartment units need their own bath and cooking facilities and 220+ sq ft [S21][S41]. That figure excludes common areas (dining, kitchen, activity space, offices), so it is a floor. The 16- and 40-unit amounts are operator estimates — verify locally.
- Utilities have a fixed base load plus a per-resident portion (operator estimates).
- The 3-year license fee is amortized monthly [S3].
- Fire alarm and sprinkler monitoring and inspections are included because the rules require the systems [S11].
- Insurance, food, supplies, software, referral fees, accounting, marketing, training and transportation are operator estimates, labeled as such.
- Franchise tax is $0 below the $2.65M threshold [S45].

### Results at 88% occupancy (monthly, approximate)
| Configuration | Revenue | Staffing incl. burden | Opex | Net | Net at 80% |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16-bed small Type B, private pay | $79,800 | $32,000 | $23,100 | about +$24,700 | +$18,400 |
| 40-unit large Type B, 20% STAR+PLUS apartments | $181,000 | $66,100 | $97,100 | about +$17,900 | +$3,800 |
| 16-bed small Type B, 6 STAR+PLUS beds | $63,200 | $32,000 | $23,100 | about +$8,100 | +$3,300 |
| 6-bed small Type B, private pay | $29,900 | $18,200 | $9,800 | about +$1,900 | about −$500 |
| 6-bed small Type B, 2 STAR+PLUS beds | $24,400 | $18,200 | $9,800 | about −$3,600 | −$5,500 |

### Sensitivity
- **Small-home price.** If a 6-bed home can only charge $4,500/month (an illustrative shared-room price, not a sourced figure), it loses about $4,300/month at 88%. The 16-bed facility still nets about $8,200.
- **Caregiver wage.** Paying attendants $15.00 instead of $13.23 cuts about $1,500/month from the 6-bed and 16-bed models: the 6-bed drops to about +$400 and the 16-bed to about +$23,100.
- **Owner as manager.** That removes about $6,370/month (salary plus burden) from a 6-bed home and lifts it to about +$8,250.
- **Each STAR+PLUS bed** in a small home gives up about $3,100/month versus private pay at the median.
- **Self-administration only.** A 6-bed home that admits only residents who self-administer medications could drop the on-call nurse (about $600/month with burden), but it narrows the market and must discharge residents whose needs change [S14].
- **40-unit building cost.** The $65,600 rent is a floor (40 studios, no common areas). Each extra $10,000/month of building cost cuts the 40-unit net to about +$7,900 at 88%; at about $83,500/month total rent it breaks even.
- **Rent.** San Antonio rent ($2,330 4-bedroom) instead of Dallas would save about $1,000/month on a 6-bed home and about $2,600 on a 16-bed [S42].

The generator calculates break-even from these inputs.
sections.risks:
- **Private-pay price risk.** The only sourced price is a median for private one-bedroom units in AL communities [S26]. Small homes with shared rooms may price lower, and the 6-bed model turns negative near $5,300/month at 88% occupancy.
- **Census volatility.** In a 6-bed home one empty bed is 17% of revenue. At 80% occupancy the private-pay 6-bed home loses about $500/month.
- **Type B night staffing.** Type B and large facilities must keep staff awake overnight [S5]. Small Type A homes avoid this cost but must discharge residents who can no longer self-evacuate [S1].
- **Pending rule rewrite.** Proposed Rule 25R031 would require dedicated staff on each shift and bar covering shortages with family members or companion care providers [S16]. Lean small-home staffing plans could need more paid hours.
- **Building costs.** New small facilities must be sprinklered and alarmed [S10][S11]. Harris County sites in a 100-year floodplain are barred for new applications [S9]. Retrofits can run tens of thousands of dollars (operator estimate).
- **Zoning.** Above six residents, or within half a mile of another community home, local approval is needed [S18][S19].
- **Medicaid rate risk.** STAR+PLUS rates are set by HHSC and paid through MCO contracts. Room and board is capped at SSI minus $85 [S22]. Each Medicaid bed earns less than half the private-pay median, and contracted facilities must accept MCO referrals when space is available [S21].
- **Wages.** Metro caregiver wages run above the statewide figures used here (Austin personal care aide median $13.64) [S30]. At $15/hour the 6-bed private-pay model nets only about $400/month.
- **Large-building cost.** The 40-unit rent ($65,600, 40 studio units at the Dallas HUD figure) excludes common areas and is a floor [S41]. The building needs about 78% occupancy to break even and nets only about $3,800/month at 80%.
- **Medication administration.** Small homes need a nurse on call (or RN delegation) to administer medications [S14]; a home without one can serve only residents who self-administer.
- **STAR+PLUS billing codes.** T2031 codes apply only from each member's ISP renewal on or after 9/1/2025; claims with the wrong code are denied [S57].
- **Workers' comp.** Coverage is elective in Texas [S38]. Non-subscribers carry injury lawsuit risk.
- **Enforcement.** A license revocation bars the owner from new licenses for five years [S9].
sections.recommendations:
1. **Lead with a 16-bed small Type B facility, mostly private pay.** It is the largest size still treated as a small facility [S2]. It spreads awake-night and manager costs over more residents and stays eligible for STAR+PLUS non-apartment contracts (freestanding, 16 or fewer beds) [S21]. The model nets about $24,700/month at 88% and $18,400 at 80%. The 40-unit apartment building nets less (about $17,900 at 88%, $3,800 at 80%) with far more capital and rent at risk.
2. **If you start with a 6-bed home, be the manager.** With a paid manager and an on-call nurse for medication administration [S14] it nets only about $1,900/month. As owner-manager (40 hrs/week on duty) [S5] it nets about $8,250. Keep it private pay and open a second home rather than adding Medicaid beds.
3. **License Type B from day one.** Residents age in place; a Type A home must discharge anyone who can't self-evacuate [S1]. Type B is also the only path to Alzheimer's certification (+$300) [S50][S3].
4. **Pick the building for the rules.** Choose a single-story building that can take an NFPA 13D/13R sprinkler system and a manual fire alarm [S10][S11]. Confirm zoning (6 or fewer by right, with half-mile spacing) [S17][S18][S19] and floodplain status in Harris County [S9]. Request an Expedited LSC inspection if timing matters [S4].
5. **Use STAR+PLUS selectively.** Contract with one or two MCOs to fill the last beds or keep residents who spend down. Cap Medicaid at about one-third of beds in a 16-bed home (about +$8,100 at 6 of 16), and get each MCO's contract rate in writing [S20][S21]. Bill T2031 only from each member's ISP renewal on or after 9/1/2025 [S57].
6. **Staff to the coming rule.** Plan dedicated, paid shift coverage without family members or shared staff, as Proposed Rule 25R031 would require [S16]. Hire medication aides with HHSC permits and an LVN on call so you can administer medications, not just assist [S14][S15].
7. **Price from local comparables.** Survey 5–10 nearby homes. If your local shared-room rate is below about $5,300 (6-bed) or $3,900 (16-bed, at 88% occupancy), rework the size or the staffing before you sign a lease.

checklist.task: Decide license type (A or B) and size (small ≤16 or large 17+)
checklist.instructions: Type A residents must self-evacuate and need no routine night attendance; Type B residents may need evacuation help or night attendance but cannot be permanently bedfast. Small = 16 or fewer, large = 17+. Most residential homes choose small Type B.

checklist.task: Decide whether you will add Alzheimer's certification
checklist.instructions: Only a Type B facility or unit can be certified (Form 3721; +$300 per 3-year license). Subchapter F adds staffing, training and construction standards.

checklist.task: Confirm owners and controlling persons are eligible
checklist.instructions: HHSC must deny an applicant if a health care, long-term care or assisted living license was revoked in any state in the last 5 years, or a person is excluded from Medicare/Medicaid. Sanctions, decertifications, evictions and unpaid judgments in the last 5 years are discretionary denial grounds.

checklist.task: Form a Texas legal entity
checklist.instructions: File a Certificate of Formation (Form 205) with the Secretary of State; $300 filing fee. The licensee on the HHSC application must match this entity exactly.

checklist.task: Obtain an EIN
checklist.instructions: Free online at irs.gov; issued the same day. Needed for payroll, banking, TULIP and Medicaid enrollment.

checklist.task: Register for Texas unemployment tax and payroll
checklist.instructions: Register with TWC once you hire. New employers pay 2.70% on the first $9,000 per worker in 2026; plus employer FICA 7.65%.

checklist.task: Decide on workers' compensation coverage
checklist.instructions: Coverage is elective in Texas. Non-subscribers carry their own injury liability; ask an insurance agent or attorney about notice duties. Get carrier quotes.

checklist.task: Plan for franchise tax reporting
checklist.instructions: Revenue at or below $2,650,000 owes no franchise tax for 2026–2027 reports, but the annual Public Information or Ownership Information Report is still filed.

checklist.task: Build a pro forma with local prices
checklist.instructions: Use local comparable prices — the statewide median of $5,666/month is for private one-bedroom units in AL communities. Model awake night staff for Type B.

checklist.task: Check zoning before signing a lease
checklist.instructions: An ALF licensed under HSC Ch. 247 qualifies as a community home if its exterior stays compatible with neighboring houses. Up to 6 persons with disabilities + 2 supervisors; no community home within one-half mile. Above 6, get local approval in writing.

checklist.task: Check the floodplain (Harris County and other counties over 3.3 million)
checklist.instructions: Initial applications in counties over 3.3 million residents must not be in a 100-year floodplain. Get the FEMA flood map or written verification from the floodplain administrator.

checklist.task: Confirm the building can meet Subchapter D for your category
checklist.instructions: Subchapter D has separate divisions for existing and new, small and large, Type A and Type B facilities. Use the 'new' division unless the building was already licensed.

checklist.task: Install a fire sprinkler system
checklist.instructions: New small Type A and Type B facilities must have an NFPA 13, 13R or 13D system, chosen per NFPA 101 Ch. 32, with electrical supervision. Get permits and fire marshal coordination.

checklist.task: Install a manual fire alarm and smoke detection
checklist.instructions: A manual fire alarm per NFPA 101 Ch. 9 with whole-building evacuation alarm. Smoke detectors in bedrooms, corridors, living and dining rooms, offices, kitchens, laundries and common areas (heat detectors allowed in kitchens and laundries). Dedicated circuit plus secondary power per NFPA 72.

checklist.task: Request early HHSC plan review for new construction or major remodels
checklist.instructions: HHSC offers architectural plan review before construction (HSC §247.0261). File the completed license application about 45 days before the building will meet LSC.
checklist.cite: HHSC How to Become an ALF Provider

checklist.task: Get local fire authority documentation
checklist.instructions: The application must include documentation from the local fire authority that the facility and its operations meet local fire ordinances.

checklist.task: If you want STAR+PLUS, design units to the setting rules
checklist.instructions: Apartment: private bath and cooking facilities, 220 sq ft single (160 remodeled), 350 sq ft per person double. Non-apartment: freestanding building licensed for 16 or fewer beds.

checklist.task: Furnish resident rooms and common areas
checklist.instructions: Budget about $2,000 per bed (operator estimate). Buy bedding, seating and dining furniture that suit residents with mobility limits.

checklist.task: Hire or designate a qualified manager
checklist.instructions: Small facility: high school diploma or equivalent. Large facility: associate's degree (nursing, health care management or related), bachelor's degree, or high school credential + 1 year of management experience. On duty 40 hrs/week.

checklist.task: Manager completes the 24-hour ALF management course
checklist.instructions: 8 hours on the assisted living standards within the first 3 months; the full 24 hours by the first anniversary as manager. Facility in-services don't count. Exempt with documentation of a comparable prior course.

checklist.task: Designate a backup for the manager in writing
checklist.instructions: An employee authorized to act in the manager's absence must be named in writing.

checklist.task: Run criminal history and registry checks before hire
checklist.instructions: Search the Nurse Aide Registry and Employee Misconduct Registry and obtain criminal history results before an employee has resident contact. Repeat registry searches annually.

checklist.task: Give every new employee 4 hours of orientation
checklist.instructions: Required before assuming any job responsibilities. Document it.

checklist.task: Give attendants 16 hours of supervised on-the-job training
checklist.instructions: Within the first 16 hours after orientation. Include first aid (Heimlich, falls, lacerations, sudden changes in condition).

checklist.task: Hire permitted medication aides and line up a nurse
checklist.instructions: Only a licensed nurse, a medication aide with an HHSC permit acting under a nurse on duty or on call, or an RN-delegated attendant may administer medications. Permit: 100 classroom + 20 lab + 10 clinical hours and exam.

checklist.task: Arrange nurse coverage for medication administration (including 6-bed homes)
checklist.instructions: Only a licensed nurse, a permitted medication aide acting under a nurse on duty or on call, or an attendant with RN delegation may administer medications. Contract or employ an LVN/RN on call (the model budgets 4 hrs/week for a 6-bed home, 8 hrs/week for 16 beds). Hours are an operator estimate — verify locally. Without nurse coverage, admit only residents who self-administer.

checklist.task: Write the staffing plan and 24-hour staffing pattern
checklist.instructions: Set ratios from residents' service plans. Type B and large facilities need awake night staff. Disclose the normal pattern before admission and post it monthly.

checklist.task: Write admission policies and the resident agreement
checklist.instructions: Cover admission criteria for your license type, services, fees, discharge and refund terms.

checklist.task: Write the medication services policy
checklist.instructions: Define administration, supervision/assistance and self-administration. Monthly counseling for self-administering residents, medication profile records, missed-dose documentation and pill-container limits.

checklist.task: Write the abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting policy
checklist.instructions: Report through TULIP or the CII hotline at 800-458-9858 within required time frames.

checklist.task: Write the emergency preparedness and response plan
checklist.instructions: Cover fire, evacuation, severe weather, power loss and heat. Train staff and run drills.

checklist.task: Write resident rights, postings and advertising policies
checklist.instructions: Resident rights, ombudsman access, required postings and rules on advertising.

checklist.task: Write resident records and retention, coordination of care and health maintenance policies
checklist.instructions: Include service plans, physician orders and coordination with home health and hospice.

checklist.task: Write the Alzheimer's/dementia training policy (even if not certified)
checklist.instructions: Facilities that are not Alzheimer's certified still have training requirements for staff caring for residents with dementia.

checklist.task: Complete HHSC's pre-licensure computer-based training
checklist.instructions: Online, about 1–2 hours, no time limit, progress is not saved. Print, sign and submit the participation certificate — packets are not accepted without it.

checklist.task: Set up a TULIP account
checklist.instructions: Applications use the HHSC online portal and prescribed forms.

checklist.task: Complete Form 3720 (and Form 3721 for Alzheimer's certification)
checklist.instructions: Form 3720 covers initial, relocation, change of ownership, capacity changes and changes of manager or controlling parties. Use 3720-G only if you meet the good-standing criteria.

checklist.task: Pay the license fee with the application
checklist.instructions: $300 + $15 per licensed bed, capped at $2,250, for a 3-year license (6 beds $390; 16 beds $540; 40 beds $900). Alzheimer's certification +$300. Nonrefundable except as allowed.

checklist.task: Respond to HHSC's completeness review
checklist.instructions: HHSC reviews within 30 days and tells you what's missing. An application still incomplete 120 days after receipt is denied.

checklist.task: Know the refund rule if HHSC misses its time frames
checklist.instructions: You may request a fee refund from the program director if processing periods are missed without good cause.

checklist.task: Notify HHSC the building is ready for the Life Safety Code inspection
checklist.instructions: Via the portal, with the application or within 120 days of HHSC receiving it. Failing 120 days after the first LSC inspection means denial.

checklist.task: Consider an Expedited LSC inspection
checklist.instructions: Submit a written request, the LSC fee and a complete application. The rule says the inspection must occur no later than the 15th day after HHSC receives the request (§553.47(g)); HHSC's How to Become an ALF Provider page says 15 business days. Check the current fee in §553.47(g) before requesting. A new fee applies to each expedited visit, including follow-ups.

checklist.task: Admit 1 to 3 residents after passing LSC
checklist.instructions: At least one and no more than three residents may be admitted before the health inspection. Notify HHSC of admissions.

checklist.task: Request and pass the health inspection
checklist.instructions: HHSC inspects for compliance with Subchapter E. Failing 120 days after the first health inspection means denial.

checklist.task: Receive the license
checklist.instructions: HHSC issues the license within 30 days after determining all requirements are met (HHSC's web page says 45 days).

checklist.task: Decide whether to serve STAR+PLUS members
checklist.instructions: Members pay room and board (SSI − $85 = $909/month in 2026) and the MCO pays a daily T2031 rate ($44.82–$74.04 by setting and level, eff. 9/1/2025).

checklist.task: Enroll in Texas Medicaid (TMHP)
checklist.instructions: States must screen and enroll all managed care network providers. Confirm whether an application fee applies to your provider type.

checklist.task: Contract with STAR+PLUS MCOs in your service area
checklist.instructions: Members must live in an ALF contracted with their MCO. The contract must state the housing options (apartment single/double, non-apartment) you will provide.

checklist.task: Set up STAR+PLUS operational duties
checklist.instructions: Health assessment and emergency training within 3 days of admission, at least 4 social activities a week, next-business-day change reports to the MCO, member trust fund records.

checklist.task: Collect room and board correctly
checklist.instructions: Room and board can't be waived (you may accept less), is prorated the first month, and is due on a written date within the month. SSI recipients owe no copayment.

checklist.task: Use the right STAR+PLUS billing code for each member (T2031 from ISP renewal)
checklist.instructions: Texas moved STAR+PLUS assisted living from RUG-III to a PDPM-based methodology on 9/1/2025. Keep billing a member's current RUG-III code until their individual service plan (ISP) renews, then bill HCPCS T2031 with the level modifier on the new ISP. Claims with the wrong code are denied. Confirm each MCO's billing guide.

checklist.task: Disclose and post the staffing pattern
checklist.instructions: Disclose the normal 24-hour staffing pattern before admission; post it monthly.

checklist.task: Deliver annual training
checklist.instructions: Direct care staff: 6 hours a year including 1 hour of fall prevention and 1 hour of behavior management. Licensed nurses, CNAs and medication aides: annual geriatric in-service.

checklist.task: Manager: 12 hours of CE every year
checklist.instructions: Must cover at least two of the listed areas (resident rights, management, accounting/budgeting, first aid, etc.). The 24-hour course counts in year one.

checklist.task: Renew medication aide permits yearly
checklist.instructions: $15 renewal. 7 hours of HHSC-approved CE for renewals after the first. Renew through TULIP.

checklist.task: Test and maintain sprinkler and alarm systems
checklist.instructions: Keep inspection and testing records for the NFPA systems required by Subchapter D.

checklist.task: Report incidents
checklist.instructions: Self-report abuse, neglect, exploitation and other reportable incidents through TULIP or 800-458-9858.

checklist.task: Renew the license on time
checklist.instructions: File the renewal at least 45 days before expiration. Late renewals pay half the basic fee extra. Fee is $300 + $15/bed per 3 years.

checklist.task: Request HHSC approval before adding beds
checklist.instructions: A capacity increase costs $15 per bed and must meet construction rules.

checklist.task: Track proposed Rule 25R031
checklist.instructions: The September 2026 proposal would require dedicated on-duty staff per shift, bar shared attendants and family coverage, add food handler and infection-control training, and renumber sections. Update policies when it is adopted.

checklist.task: Pay any HHSC trust fund assessment
checklist.instructions: HHSC may charge annual fees to keep the ALF trust fund at up to $500,000. Pay within 90 days of notice.

corrections_vs_previous: The old checklist told applicants to file Form 2026 for 'Administrator Training Approval'. That form is for home and community support services agencies (HCSSAs), not ALFs. ALF managers complete a 24-hour assisted living management course under 26 TAC §553.253.

The old checklist cited rule sections that don't exist or don't say what it claimed: §553.15 (financial/insurance), §553.51 (ownership), §553.41 (medication), §553.251 (health department) and §553.28 (TAS review). Chapter 553 Subchapter B ends at §553.47, and the sections reviewed contain no insurance or financial-reserve requirement.

The old checklist said to attach fire marshal and local 'health department' pass certificates and insurance and bank statements to the application. The rule requires documentation from the local fire authority (§553.19). HHSC itself performs the Life Safety Code and health inspections after the application is filed, and you may admit 1–3 residents between them (§553.23).
The old checklist described Type C as for '4+ unrelated residents in small home'. HHSC accepts Type C (four-bed) applications for renewals only; new operators license Type A or Type B.

The old market report never explained the Type A vs Type B night rule. Type B and large Type A facilities must keep night staff awake (§553.253). That is the biggest cost driver in a small home, and the old P&L ignored it.

The old report quoted a Dallas average of $4,200/month and small-home rates of $5,000–$7,500 with no verifiable source. CareScout 2025 puts the Texas median at $5,666/month for a private one-bedroom in an AL community.

The old report omitted STAR+PLUS entirely. Texas Medicaid assisted living is paid through STAR+PLUS MCOs at published T2031 rates ($44.82–$74.04/day, eff. 9/1/2025) plus resident room and board of SSI − $85 ($909/month in 2026).

The old report said HHSC issues the license 'within about 45 days of final approvals'. Rule §553.21 sets 30 days after all requirements are met, after a 30-day completeness review, with denial at 120 days if incomplete.

The old report projected $80k–$110k a year of profit on a 6-bed home with a paid caregiver budget of $150k–$180k and no paid manager. The rule requires a manager on duty 40 hours a week. At the sourced median price with a paid manager and an on-call nurse the model nets about $1,900/month (about $22k a year).

The old report stated Texas requires CO detectors in ALFs, room sizes (80/100 sq ft), one toilet per 6 residents and no more than 4 residents per bedroom without citations. These are not repeated here; verify them in Subchapter D for your facility category.
